```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

# Little brown bat detections (same data as the pre-class videos)
bats <- read_csv("../pre-class/data/5bat_count_data-21682.csv") |>
  filter(Species == "Myotis lucifugus")
bats_by_year <- bats |>
  summarize(p_detected = mean(detected), .by = Year)

bat_glm <- glm(detected ~ Year, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = bats)
bat_pred_grid <- tibble(Year = seq(2003, 2019, length.out = 101))
bat_pred_grid$p_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  type = "response",
  newdata = bat_pred_grid
)

bat_b0 <- signif(coef(bat_glm)[["(Intercept)"]], 4)
bat_b1 <- signif(coef(bat_glm)[["Year"]], 4)
bat_p <- \(year) {
  signif(predict(bat_glm, tibble(Year = year), type = "response"), 2)
}

# Jittered raw data with a binned summary, as in the live coding
bat_plot <- ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2, seed = 1),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("Detected", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))
```

# Logistic regression

## Today's agenda

- **Review** logistic regression (10 min)
- **Recap** the white-nose syndrome example (15 min)
- **Kick** field goals and model them (35 min)
- **Recap** (10 min)

# Review

## Which response calls for logistic regression?

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**A.** Soil lead (ppm) at a property

[**B.** Whether soil lead at a property exceeds the EPA threshold]{.fragment .highlight-green fragment-index=1}

**C.** Number of properties in a neighborhood with soil lead above the EPA threshold

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="font-size:0.75em"}

- Logistic regression is for **binary** responses: yes/no, 0/1, success/failure.
- A is continuous, so use linear regression.
- C is a count. It's built from binary outcomes, but it isn't one itself. (More on counts later.)

:::

## True or false?

> Logistic regression is necessary when there's a binary **predictor** variable.

::: {.fragment}

**False**

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

- The kind of model depends on the **response**, not the predictors.
- A binary predictor is a categorical variable with two levels. It becomes a dummy variable (0 or 1) in a linear regression, like we did in weeks 4-6.

:::

## Which is a valid logistic regression?

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

[**A.** $\quad \text{Bleached} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \qquad \text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PeakSST}$]{.fragment .highlight-green fragment-index=1}

**B.** $\quad \text{Bleached} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \qquad p = \text{logit}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PeakSST})$

**C.** $\quad \text{Bleached} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\text{logit}(p)) \qquad p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PeakSST}$

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="font-size:0.7em"}

- The logit turns a **probability** into log odds, so it goes on $p$.
- B applies the logit to the linear part, which can be any value. The logit of 3 or -2 doesn't exist.
- C makes $p$ a straight line, which can go below 0 or above 1. Bernoulli also needs a probability, not log odds.

:::

## Why do we need the logit link?

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**A.** It transforms the response variable

**B.** It makes the residuals normally distributed

[**C.** It transforms $(0, 1)$ to $(-\infty, \infty)$]{.fragment .highlight-green fragment-index=1}

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="font-size:0.75em"}

- **Not A**: it transforms $p$, the _probability_ of the response. The responses are all 0s and 1s, and $\text{logit}(0)$ and $\text{logit}(1)$ are $-\infty$ and $\infty$.
- **Not B**: the Bernoulli distribution describes how the 0s and 1s vary. No normal distribution is involved.
- **C**: the linear part, $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, can be any number. The logit connects it to a valid probability.

:::

# White-nose syndrome

## Has the little brown bat declined?

White-nose syndrome reached West Virginia in 2009. Each point is one survey of one site in one year.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

bat_plot
```

## Has the little brown bat declined?

The line is the proportion of sites with detections each year.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

bat_plot +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bats_by_year,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  )
```

## Write the model

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

- What's the response? Is it continuous or binary?
  - **Detected**: binary. 1 if any little brown bats were counted.
- What distribution describes a binary response?
  - **Bernoulli**, with probability of success $p$.
- What do we want to change with Year?
  - $p$, the probability of detection.
- How do we link $p$ to a linear equation?
  - The **logit**.

:::

## Write the model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Detected} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Year}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

- Line 1: each survey is a 0 or 1, and the chance of a 1 is $p$.
- Line 2: the log odds of $p$ change linearly with Year.

:::

## Fit the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

bat_glm <- glm(
  detected ~ Year,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = bats
)
summary(bat_glm)
```

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
#| class-output: small-output

summary(bat_glm)$coefficients
```

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

$$
\text{logit}(p) = `r bat_b0` - `r abs(bat_b1)` \text{Year}
$$

Each year, the log odds of detection fall by `r abs(bat_b1)`. In probabilities: `r bat_p(2003)` in 2003 and `r bat_p(2019)` in 2019.

:::

## Visualize the model

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

bat_plot +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_pred_grid,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  )
```

The model's predicted probability of detection, on top of the raw data.

# Field goal!

## Your turn to collect the data

Does the chance of kicking a field goal depend on distance?

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

1. **Fold** a paper football (next slide)
2. **Generate** a random distance between 10 and 50 cm: `sample(10:50, 1)` in R
3. **Kick**: your partner makes goal posts with their hands at the edge of the table. Flick the football from your distance. It's good if it goes between the posts.
4. **Record** your distance and whether you made it on the [Google Form](https://forms.gle/rwjyWQL2MhRDGvP89)

:::

## Fold a paper football

![](images/paper-football.png)

## Kick a field goal

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

1. **Form pairs**
2. **Generate random distances** between 10 and 50 cm: `sample(10:50, 1)` in R
3. **Take turns kicking**: one partner makes goal posts with their hands, the other flicks the football from their distance
4. **Submit your results** on the Google Form (link on Slack)

:::

## On your handout

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

1. **Draw** the data
2. **Write** the model in statistical notation
3. We'll fit the model in R. **Write down** the coefficients.
4. **Draw** $\text{logit}(p)$ vs. distance (the linear part)
5. **Calculate** $p$ for distances of 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 cm
6. **Draw** $p$ vs. distance

:::

## Fit the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

sheet_url <- "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1mxNglhoIY9Kdlnmm0PCk3b8cP_l_27CTTBf2Fyek7bI/export?format=csv"
field_goals <- read_csv(sheet_url) |>
  # Column C is distance, column D is whether the kick was good
  select(dist_cm = 3, made_it = 4) |>
  mutate(success = as.integer(made_it == "Yes"))

fg_glm <- glm(
  success ~ dist_cm,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = field_goals
)
coef(fg_glm)
```

# Recap

## Key points

::: {.fragment}

**How do we model a binary response?**

As a Bernoulli variable, where the probability of success, $p$, changes with the predictors.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**What does the logit do?**

It connects $p$, which is between 0 and 1, to a linear equation, which can be any value. It transforms $p$, not the 0s and 1s.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**How do we interpret the coefficients?**

They're in log odds. Convert to probabilities at a few predictor values, then plot the predictions.

:::

## One more look at your handout

Compare your $p$ at 10 and 20 cm with your $p$ at 30 and 40 cm.

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

- Each step adds the same 10 cm, and logit(p) changes by the same amount ($10 \beta_1$) each time.
- Does $p$ change by the same amount each time?
- A straight line on the log odds scale is an S-curve on the probability scale. A step in distance changes $p$ the most near $p = 0.5$ and the least near 0 or 1.

:::
